ui.hardwareSourcesText: Hardware Security Foundations contains original explanations and exercises informed by selected sections of The Hardware Hacking Handbook, by Jasper van Woudenberg and Colin O’Flynn, with additional introductory electronics background. The book’s text, figures, and exercises are not reproduced here.

hw-unit-04.title: Understanding an unfamiliar device
hw-unit-04.description: Identify components, research documentation, and examine firmware.

hw-u1-concept-01.title: What is an embedded system?
hw-u1-concept-01.body: An embedded system is a computer built into a device to perform a particular function. It receives inputs, processes information, and controls outputs.
hw-u1-concept-01.example: A washing machine reads buttons and water sensors, then controls its motor and valves.
hw-u1-concept-01.takeaway: An embedded system is a computer built into a device to perform a particular function.

hw-u1-concept-02.title: Following information through a device
hw-u1-concept-02.body: A sensor measures something, a processor makes decisions, and an actuator performs a physical action.
hw-u1-concept-02.example: In an automatic door, a motion sensor detects a person, a processor decides to open the door, and a motor moves it.
hw-u1-concept-02.takeaway: A sensor measures something, a processor makes decisions, and an actuator performs a physical action..

hw-u1-concept-03.title: Remembering after power is removed
hw-u1-concept-03.body: Volatile memory, such as ordinary RAM, needs power to retain its contents. Nonvolatile memory, such as flash, retains data without power.
hw-u1-concept-03.example: A sensor might keep its current calculations in RAM and its saved configuration in flash.
hw-u1-concept-03.takeaway: Volatile memory, such as ordinary RAM, needs power to retain its contents.

hw-u1-concept-04.title: Recognizing firmware
hw-u1-concept-04.body: Firmware is software that controls a device’s operation. It is commonly stored in nonvolatile memory. Stored measurements and settings are data, rather than necessarily being firmware.
hw-u1-concept-04.example: A digital scale’s measurement program is firmware; its saved calibration value is configuration data.
hw-u1-concept-04.takeaway: Firmware is software that controls a device’s operation.

hw-u1-concept-05.title: Understanding startup
hw-u1-concept-05.body: Devices often start in stages. Initial boot code runs first, a bootloader prepares or loads the next software stage, and the main firmware starts afterward. Exact arrangements vary.
hw-u1-concept-05.example: In one device: initial boot code → bootloader → application firmware.

hw-u1-concept-06.title: Identifying an asset
hw-u1-concept-06.body: A security asset is something valuable that needs protection. Assets can include secret keys, personal information, firmware, or the ability to operate correctly.
hw-u1-concept-06.example: In a payment terminal, a secret authentication key is an asset. A connector is a possible access point to the system.
hw-u1-concept-06.takeaway: A security asset is something valuable that needs protection.

hw-u1-concept-07.title: Protecting confidentiality
hw-u1-concept-07.body: Confidentiality means preventing unauthorized disclosure. An attacker can violate confidentiality simply by reading information, without changing it.
hw-u1-concept-07.example: Copying private location records from a tracker breaks confidentiality even if the original records remain intact.

hw-u1-concept-08.title: Protecting integrity
hw-u1-concept-08.body: Integrity concerns preventing or detecting unauthorized changes. Confidentiality protects against disclosure; integrity protects against alteration.
hw-u1-concept-08.example: Secretly changing a recorded temperature from 80°C to 30°C violates the integrity of the measurement.
hw-u1-concept-08.takeaway: Integrity concerns preventing or detecting unauthorized changes.

hw-u1-concept-09.title: Authenticating firmware
hw-u1-concept-09.body: Firmware authentication checks whether software comes from an authorized source and has not been altered. A digital signature can support this check when verified using a trusted key. Encryption alone does not establish who authorized the firmware.
hw-u1-concept-09.example: A device rejects an update whose signature cannot be verified using its trusted update key.
hw-u1-concept-09.takeaway: Firmware authentication checks whether software comes from an authorized source and has not been altered.

hw-u1-concept-10.title: Considering the attacker’s access
hw-u1-concept-10.body: An attacker profile describes capabilities such as access, time, equipment, and expertise. Different capabilities make different attack paths possible.
hw-u1-concept-10.example: A remote attacker may send network requests. Someone holding the device may also reach internal connectors.
hw-u1-concept-10.takeaway: An attacker profile describes capabilities such as access, time, equipment, and expertise.

hw-u1-concept-11.title: Recognizing multiple access paths
hw-u1-concept-11.body: An attack surface includes the ways someone can interact with a system and potentially affect its security. Network services and physical interfaces can both contribute.
hw-u1-concept-11.example: Turning off Bluetooth removes one communication path, but it does not automatically disable an internal maintenance connector.
hw-u1-concept-11.takeaway: An attack surface includes the ways someone can interact with a system and potentially affect its security.

hw-u1-concept-12.title: Stating a useful threat
hw-u1-concept-12.body: A useful threat scenario connects an attacker’s capabilities, an asset, and an unwanted outcome. This makes the problem specific enough to evaluate.
hw-u1-concept-12.example: “A visitor with temporary access could alter a sensor’s calibration through its maintenance interface” identifies access, an asset, and an outcome.
hw-u1-concept-12.takeaway: A useful threat scenario connects an attacker’s capabilities, an asset, and an unwanted outcome.

hw-u1-concept-13.title: Understanding alternative attack paths
hw-u1-concept-13.body: An attack tree breaks a goal into smaller steps. At an OR node, any one child path is sufficient to achieve the parent goal.
hw-u1-concept-13.example: If a file can be obtained from either an unprotected backup or an exposed storage device, securing only the backup leaves another path.
hw-u1-concept-13.takeaway: An attack tree breaks a goal into smaller steps.

hw-u1-concept-14.title: Understanding required combinations
hw-u1-concept-14.body: At an AND node, every listed condition is required for that modeled path. Blocking one necessary condition stops that path, although other paths may still exist.
hw-u1-concept-14.example: A particular maintenance operation requires both physical access and a valid service credential.
hw-u1-concept-14.takeaway: At an AND node, every listed condition is required for that modeled path.

hw-u1-concept-15.title: Combining protection, detection, and response
hw-u1-concept-15.body: Security measures can protect against an event, detect that it occurred, or respond to it. These roles complement each other.
hw-u1-concept-15.example: A locked enclosure provides protection; an opening sensor provides detection; a configured action following an alarm provides response.
hw-u1-concept-15.takeaway: Security measures can protect against an event, detect that it occurred, or respond to it.

hw-u2-concept-01.title: Understanding voltage
hw-u2-concept-01.body: Voltage is an electrical potential difference between two points. A voltage measurement therefore needs a reference point.
hw-u2-concept-01.example: Saying a supply is “3.3 V” usually means its supply pin is 3.3 V above the designated ground reference.
hw-u2-concept-01.takeaway: Voltage is an electrical potential difference between two points.

hw-u2-concept-02.title: Understanding current
hw-u2-concept-02.body: Current is the rate of electric charge flow, measured in amperes. A power supply’s current rating usually states its capacity, rather than a fixed current it forces through every load.
hw-u2-concept-02.example: A suitable 5 V supply rated for up to 2 A can power a device drawing 0.1 A.
hw-u2-concept-02.takeaway: Current is the rate of electric charge flow, measured in amperes.

hw-u2-concept-03.title: Understanding resistance
hw-u2-concept-03.body: Resistance opposes current flow. For an ideal resistor at a fixed voltage, increasing resistance decreases current.
hw-u2-concept-03.example: At the same voltage, a 2 kΩ resistor carries less current than a 1 kΩ resistor.

hw-u2-concept-04.title: Applying Ohm’s law
hw-u2-concept-04.body: Ohm’s law relates voltage, current, and resistance. With volts and ohms, the current is in amperes.
hw-u2-concept-04.example: A 3 V difference across 3,000 Ω gives 3 / 3000 = 0.001 A, or 1 mA.
hw-u2-concept-04.takeaway: Ohm’s law relates voltage, current, and resistance.

hw-u2-concept-05.title: Relating voltage and current to power
hw-u2-concept-05.body: Electrical power describes the rate of energy transfer. For steady DC conditions, power equals voltage multiplied by current and is measured in watts.
hw-u2-concept-05.example: A device drawing 0.1 A at 3 V receives 3 × 0.1 = 0.3 W.
hw-u2-concept-05.takeaway: Electrical power describes the rate of energy transfer.

hw-u2-concept-06.title: Sharing a reference
hw-u2-concept-06.body: For a simple, non-isolated connection using single-ended signals, devices need a compatible reference. Otherwise, the receiver may interpret a signal’s voltage incorrectly.
hw-u2-concept-06.example: A transmitter describes a signal relative to its ground; the receiver evaluates that signal relative to its own ground.
hw-u2-concept-06.takeaway: For a simple, non-isolated connection using single-ended signals, devices need a compatible reference.

hw-u2-concept-07.title: Interpreting logic levels
hw-u2-concept-07.body: Digital inputs recognize voltage ranges as LOW or HIGH. Voltages between the guaranteed ranges may have an undefined interpretation.
hw-u2-concept-07.example: If LOW is guaranteed at or below 0.8 V and HIGH at or above 2.0 V, then 0.4 V is LOW and 2.5 V is HIGH.
hw-u2-concept-07.takeaway: Digital inputs recognize voltage ranges as LOW or HIGH.

hw-u2-concept-08.title: Checking electrical compatibility
hw-u2-concept-08.body: Recognizing a voltage as HIGH and tolerating that voltage are different requirements. An input’s absolute maximum rating is a limit, not a recommended operating voltage.
hw-u2-concept-08.example: A signal may be high enough to represent HIGH while still exceeding what the receiving pin can tolerate.
hw-u2-concept-08.takeaway: Recognizing a voltage as HIGH and tolerating that voltage are different requirements.

hw-u2-concept-09.title: Recognizing a floating input
hw-u2-concept-09.body: A high-impedance input draws little current and does not establish its own voltage. If nothing drives or biases it, it can float and respond unpredictably to noise.
hw-u2-concept-09.example: An unconnected input might alternate between HIGH and LOW even though no deliberate signal is being sent.
hw-u2-concept-09.takeaway: A high-impedance input draws little current and does not establish its own voltage.

hw-u2-concept-10.title: Giving a released line a defined state
hw-u2-concept-10.body: A pull-up resistor biases a line HIGH when no device pulls it LOW. An open-drain output can pull LOW or release the line; it does not actively drive HIGH.
hw-u2-concept-10.example: With a suitable pull-up, a released open-drain line rises HIGH. When its output pulls LOW, the line becomes LOW.
hw-u2-concept-10.takeaway: A pull-up resistor biases a line HIGH when no device pulls it LOW.

hw-u2-concept-11.title: Measuring a supply voltage
hw-u2-concept-11.body: A multimeter in voltage mode measures the potential difference between its probes. To measure a supply rail relative to ground, the probes go across those two points.
hw-u2-concept-11.example: On a suitable low-voltage circuit, a 3.3 V rail is checked with the voltage probe on the rail and the reference probe on ground.
hw-u2-concept-11.takeaway: A multimeter in voltage mode measures the potential difference between its probes.

hw-u2-concept-12.title: Interpreting continuity
hw-u2-concept-12.body: Continuity mode checks for a low-resistance path. Use it on a de-energized circuit with stored energy safely discharged. A beep does not by itself reveal the exact path through the circuit.
hw-u2-concept-12.example: Two points may show continuity through a wire, a PCB trace, or another low-resistance route.
hw-u2-concept-12.takeaway: Continuity mode checks for a low-resistance path.

hw-u2-concept-13.title: Finding a brief voltage disturbance
hw-u2-concept-13.body: An oscilloscope displays voltage over time. A multimeter’s normal display may miss short events that occur between updates or are averaged into its reading.
hw-u2-concept-13.example: A supply can usually read 3.3 V while briefly dipping during startup. An appropriately configured oscilloscope can reveal that dip.
hw-u2-concept-13.takeaway: An oscilloscope displays voltage over time.

hw-u2-concept-14.title: Choosing a logic analyzer
hw-u2-concept-14.body: A logic analyzer records digital states across time, often on several channels. An oscilloscope shows the analog waveform, including its voltage shape.
hw-u2-concept-14.example: Use an oscilloscope to inspect overshoot on one signal. Use a logic analyzer to compare the HIGH/LOW sequence of several compatible signals.
hw-u2-concept-14.takeaway: A logic analyzer records digital states across time, often on several channels.

hw-u2-concept-15.title: Recognizing a missed event
hw-u2-concept-15.body: A sampled instrument observes a signal at discrete times. A pulse shorter than the interval between samples can occur entirely between them and be missed.
hw-u2-concept-15.example: If samples occur every 10 microseconds, a 2-microsecond pulse could start and finish between consecutive samples.
hw-u2-concept-15.takeaway: A sampled instrument observes a signal at discrete times.

hw-u3-concept-01.title: A connector is not a protocol
hw-u3-concept-01.body: A connector provides physical contact points. A protocol defines how devices communicate. Two connectors with the same shape can use different signals and pin assignments.
hw-u3-concept-01.example: Two boards each have four pins. One uses a serial interface; the other exposes power and programming signals. Their matching shape does not establish compatibility.
hw-u3-concept-01.takeaway: A connector provides physical contact points.

hw-u3-concept-02.title: UART transmit and receive
hw-u3-concept-02.body: A basic UART connection has a transmit signal, TX, and a receive signal, RX. One device’s transmitter connects to the other’s receiver. Compatible signal voltages and a common reference are also needed. UART does not require a separate shared clock wire.
hw-u3-concept-02.example: To send information from device A to device B, connect A’s TX to B’s RX.
hw-u3-concept-02.takeaway: A basic UART connection has a transmit signal, TX, and a receive signal, RX.

hw-u3-concept-03.title: Matching UART timing
hw-u3-concept-03.body: UART devices must agree on communication settings, including the baud rate, which describes the signalling rate. For ordinary binary UART, it corresponds to the number of transmitted bits per second.
hw-u3-concept-03.example: A board transmits at 9,600 baud. An adapter configured for 115,200 baud samples using the wrong timing and may display unreadable characters.
hw-u3-concept-03.takeaway: UART devices must agree on communication settings, including the baud rate, which describes the signalling rate.

hw-u3-concept-04.title: Unreadable output is not a diagnosis
hw-u3-concept-04.body: Unreadable UART output can result from incorrect timing or framing settings. It can also be binary data rather than text. Unreadable characters alone do not prove that information is encrypted.
hw-u3-concept-04.example: A sensor sends binary measurements. A terminal displays symbols because it tries to interpret those bytes as text.
hw-u3-concept-04.takeaway: Unreadable UART output can result from incorrect timing or framing settings.

hw-u3-concept-05.title: SPI uses a shared clock
hw-u3-concept-05.body: SPI is a synchronous interface: a controller supplies a clock that coordinates data transfer. A typical four-wire SPI connection also has separate data paths in each direction and a target-selection signal.
hw-u3-concept-05.example: A processor supplies clock pulses while exchanging data with a sensor. Both use those pulses to coordinate when bits are transferred.
hw-u3-concept-05.takeaway: SPI is a synchronous interface: a controller supplies a clock that coordinates data transfer.

hw-u3-concept-06.title: Selecting an SPI target
hw-u3-concept-06.body: In a common SPI arrangement, several targets share clock and data wires but have separate chip-select signals. The controller selects the intended target. Chip select is often active-low, meaning LOW selects the device.
hw-u3-concept-06.example: Two sensors share a bus. Pulling sensor A’s active-low select LOW while keeping sensor B’s HIGH selects A.
hw-u3-concept-06.takeaway: In a common SPI arrangement, several targets share clock and data wires but have separate chip-select signals.

hw-u3-concept-07.title: Selecting the correct SPI mode
hw-u3-concept-07.body: SPI settings specify the clock’s idle level and which clock edge is used to sample data. Together, these define the SPI mode. A decoder configured incorrectly can misread a valid transfer.
hw-u3-concept-07.example: A device expects data to be sampled on falling edges. A decoder sampling on rising edges may interpret changing data incorrectly.
hw-u3-concept-07.takeaway: SPI settings specify the clock’s idle level and which clock edge is used to sample data.

hw-u3-concept-08.title: I²C’s two shared signals
hw-u3-concept-08.body: I²C uses SDA for data and SCL for the clock. In ordinary Standard/Fast-mode I²C, devices pull these lines LOW or release them; pull-up resistors provide the HIGH level.
hw-u3-concept-08.example: When every device releases SDA, its pull-up brings the line HIGH. A device sends a LOW by pulling it down.
hw-u3-concept-08.takeaway: I²C uses SDA for data and SCL for the clock.

hw-u3-concept-09.title: I²C addresses
hw-u3-concept-09.body: An I²C controller normally selects a target by transmitting its address. If two targets on the same bus have the same active address, ordinary addressed transfers cannot select them individually.
hw-u3-concept-09.example: Two identical sensors both use address 0x40. Changing one to a supported alternative address lets the controller address them separately.
hw-u3-concept-09.takeaway: An I²C controller normally selects a target by transmitting its address.

hw-u3-concept-10.title: What an acknowledgement tells you
hw-u3-concept-10.body: An I²C acknowledgement, or ACK, is a response within a transfer. An address ACK indicates that something acknowledged that address. It does not authenticate the device or prove that a later application-level operation succeeded.
hw-u3-concept-10.example: A target acknowledges its address, but a later command is unsupported. The first acknowledgement does not establish that the command worked.
hw-u3-concept-10.takeaway: An I²C acknowledgement, or ACK, is a response within a transfer.

hw-u3-concept-11.title: Distinguishing bus arrangements
hw-u3-concept-11.body: Interface identification should combine observations. Shared data and clock wires with separate target-select wires suggest a typical SPI arrangement. Shared SDA/SCL wires with address-based selection suggest I²C.
hw-u3-concept-11.example: Three sensors share two communication lines, and the controller sends different addresses. That supports an I²C interpretation.

hw-u3-concept-12.title: CAN uses a differential pair
hw-u3-concept-12.body: High-speed CAN uses a differential pair, CANH and CANL. A receiver interprets the voltage difference between them. A CAN transceiver converts between this bus signalling and a controller’s logic-level transmit/receive signals.
hw-u3-concept-12.example: A CAN interface uses a transceiver to connect to CANH/CANL; those bus wires are not simply UART TX and RX.
hw-u3-concept-12.takeaway: High-speed CAN uses a differential pair, CANH and CANL.

hw-u3-concept-13.title: USB identification is a reported description
hw-u3-concept-13.body: In a USB connection, the host discovers and configures a device through enumeration. The device supplies descriptors containing information such as identifiers and supported functions. This information describes what the device reports; it is not, by itself, proof of authenticity.
hw-u3-concept-13.example: A USB device reports that it provides a serial-port function. The host uses that information to select suitable software.
hw-u3-concept-13.takeaway: In a USB connection, the host discovers and configures a device through enumeration.

hw-u3-concept-14.title: An SD-related interface is not always storage
hw-u3-concept-14.body: eMMC is managed flash storage with an integrated controller. SDIO allows an SD-style interface to communicate with input/output devices, including some wireless modules. An SD-related interface therefore does not automatically identify a storage chip.
hw-u3-concept-14.example: A processor communicates with a Wi-Fi module over SDIO. The interface carries communication with the radio rather than serving as a general storage device.
hw-u3-concept-14.takeaway: eMMC is managed flash storage with an integrated controller.

hw-u3-concept-15.title: Capturing a parallel bus
hw-u3-concept-15.body: A parallel bus carries multiple bits on separate data lines during the same transfer. To reconstruct a complete value, a capture needs the relevant data lines and the timing/control signals that establish when the value is valid.
hw-u3-concept-15.example: An eight-bit bus transfers a byte across eight data lines. Observing only one line reveals only that line’s contribution.
hw-u3-concept-15.takeaway: A parallel bus carries multiple bits on separate data lines during the same transfer.

hw-u3-concept-16.title: JTAG testing and debugging
hw-u3-concept-16.body: JTAG can provide boundary scan, which helps test chip connections through special internal test circuitry. Some processors also expose debugging through JTAG. Available functions depend on the chip and its configuration.
hw-u3-concept-16.example: A board permits a boundary-scan test but restricts processor debugging. Connection testing does not establish unrestricted access to memory.
hw-u3-concept-16.takeaway: JTAG can provide boundary scan, which helps test chip connections through special internal test circuitry.

hw-u3-concept-17.title: Choosing capture equipment
hw-u3-concept-17.body: Capture equipment must support both the electrical signals and the timing of an interface. A suitable channel count alone is insufficient. Fast signals may require greater bandwidth, appropriate probes and a protocol-specific analyser.
hw-u3-concept-17.example: An analyser has enough channels for a bus, but its sampling rate misses short transitions. The resulting capture cannot reliably describe all bus activity.
hw-u3-concept-17.takeaway: Capture equipment must support both the electrical signals and the timing of an interface.

hw-u3-concept-18.title: Combining interface evidence
hw-u3-concept-18.body: A reliable interface identification combines electrical measurements, wiring observations and protocol behaviour. A label or pin count is a useful clue, but several consistent observations support a stronger conclusion.
hw-u3-concept-18.example: A connector labelled “SERIAL” becomes a stronger UART candidate when measurements show compatible logic levels, separate transmit/receive paths and no shared clock.
hw-u3-concept-18.takeaway: A reliable interface identification combines electrical measurements, wiring observations and protocol behaviour.

hw-u4-concept-01.title: Identify the exact device
hw-u4-concept-01.body: Devices sold under the same product name can have different hardware revisions. Record the model, board revision and visible identifiers before choosing documentation.
hw-u4-concept-01.example: Two routers share a product name, but revision A and revision B use different processors. A revision-A diagram may not describe revision B.
hw-u4-concept-01.takeaway: Devices sold under the same product name can have different hardware revisions.

hw-u4-concept-02.title: Record the original arrangement
hw-u4-concept-02.body: Clear photographs and notes preserve information about connector positions, cable orientation and component locations. Record the original arrangement before making changes.
hw-u4-concept-02.example: Before disconnecting two similar cables, you photograph their positions and label their destinations.
hw-u4-concept-02.takeaway: Clear photographs and notes preserve information about connector positions, cable orientation and component locations.

hw-u4-concept-03.title: Use component markings as evidence
hw-u4-concept-03.body: Printed chip markings can help identify a component. Markings may be abbreviated, so check the manufacturer’s documentation and compare the package and pin count before accepting a match.
hw-u4-concept-03.example: A marking search returns two candidates. Only one has a package and pin count matching the board.
hw-u4-concept-03.takeaway: Printed chip markings can help identify a component.

hw-u4-concept-04.title: Package shape does not establish function
hw-u4-concept-04.body: A chip’s package describes its physical form and connections. For example, a BGA package has a grid of connection balls underneath. Package type alone does not tell you whether a chip is a processor, memory or another component.
hw-u4-concept-04.example: Two BGA chips on a board may perform different functions even though both connect through balls beneath their bodies.
hw-u4-concept-04.takeaway: A chip’s package describes its physical form and connections.

hw-u4-concept-05.title: Read pinouts in the correct orientation
hw-u4-concept-05.body: A pinout drawing has a defined viewing direction, such as top view or bottom view. Locate the package’s orientation marker and use the drawing’s stated view before assigning pin numbers.
hw-u4-concept-05.example: Looking through the board from underneath reverses the apparent arrangement compared with a top-view drawing.
hw-u4-concept-05.takeaway: A pinout drawing has a defined viewing direction, such as top view or bottom view.

hw-u4-concept-06.title: Interpret continuity cautiously
hw-u4-concept-06.body: With a circuit de-energised, a continuity test can help find low-resistance connections. A beep does not necessarily prove a direct copper trace: an in-circuit path can pass through components.
hw-u4-concept-06.example: Two pads produce a continuity indication because a low-value resistor connects them. They are not joined by an uninterrupted trace.
hw-u4-concept-06.takeaway: With a circuit de-energised, a continuity test can help find low-resistance connections.

hw-u4-concept-07.title: Build a map with confidence levels
hw-u4-concept-07.body: A useful board map records both connections and the evidence supporting them. Distinguish confirmed observations from hypotheses so uncertain information does not become an assumed fact.
hw-u4-concept-07.example: A trace visibly connects a processor pin to a resistor. Its continuation disappears inside the board, so you mark the destination as unconfirmed.
hw-u4-concept-07.takeaway: A useful board map records both connections and the evidence supporting them.

hw-u4-concept-08.title: Compare documents with the actual board
hw-u4-concept-08.body: Schematics, regulatory photographs and other documents can provide useful leads. They may describe another revision, so compare them with the physical board before transferring conclusions.
hw-u4-concept-08.example: A regulatory photograph shows a debug connector that is absent from your revision. The photograph remains useful, but it does not establish that your board has the same connector.
hw-u4-concept-08.takeaway: Schematics, regulatory photographs and other documents can provide useful leads.

hw-u4-concept-09.title: An update file may be a container
hw-u4-concept-09.body: A firmware update download may contain headers, signatures, compressed sections or several images. It is not necessarily a raw copy of the bytes stored on one flash chip.
hw-u4-concept-09.example: An update package contains a bootloader image, an application image and installation metadata. Its total contents differ from a simple application-memory dump.
hw-u4-concept-09.takeaway: A firmware update download may contain headers, signatures, compressed sections or several images.

hw-u4-concept-10.title: Preserve the original and check copies
hw-u4-concept-10.body: Keep an unchanged original and analyse a working copy. A cryptographic hash acts as a fingerprint of file contents. Matching SHA-256 hashes provide strong evidence that two files contain the same bytes; they do not prove who created those bytes.
hw-u4-concept-10.example: You hash a downloaded file and its working copy. Matching results support that the copy preserved the original contents.
hw-u4-concept-10.takeaway: Keep an unchanged original and analyse a working copy.

hw-u4-concept-11.title: Interpret strings and entropy as clues
hw-u4-concept-11.body: Readable strings can suggest features but may come from unused code. Entropy describes how varied or unpredictable byte values appear; high entropy can occur in compressed or encrypted data. Neither clue proves a feature is active or identifies a format by itself.
hw-u4-concept-11.example: An image contains “debug console” and a high-entropy section. Those observations suggest investigation, but do not establish an accessible console or encrypted storage.
hw-u4-concept-11.takeaway: Readable strings can suggest features but may come from unused code.

hw-u4-concept-12.title: Combine evidence without overstating access
hw-u4-concept-12.body: Distinguish a chip’s possible capabilities, the board’s observed behaviour and the access actually demonstrated. Datasheets describe supported functions; labels and firmware strings provide clues; direct observations establish narrower facts about the tested configuration.
hw-u4-concept-12.example: A processor supports debugging, but the product disables it. The processor’s capability does not establish that debugging is available on that product.
hw-u4-concept-12.takeaway: Distinguish a chip’s possible capabilities, the board’s observed behaviour and the access actually demonstrated.

hw-u1-concept-16.title: Understanding attack effort
hw-u1-concept-16.body: An attacker needs time, equipment and knowledge. Increasing the effort required can make an attack less attractive, even when it remains possible.
hw-u1-concept-16.example: Recovering a secret originally took ten minutes. A defence makes it take several days. The defence increases the attacker’s effort without proving that recovery is impossible.
hw-u1-concept-16.takeaway: An attacker needs time, equipment and knowledge.

hw-u1-concept-17.title: Knowing which verification key to trust
hw-u1-concept-17.body: A digital signature is useful only when the device trusts the verification key. A root of trust provides the trusted starting point for deciding which keys or software to accept.
hw-u1-concept-17.example: An attacker supplies modified software and their own verification key. The signature matches that key, but the device rejects it because the key is not authorised.
hw-u1-concept-17.takeaway: A digital signature is useful only when the device trusts the verification key.

hw-u1-concept-18.title: Continuing the checks during startup
hw-u1-concept-18.body: A chain of trust connects startup stages through verification. Trusted initial code checks the next stage, which checks the following stage before running it.
hw-u1-concept-18.example: Boot ROM verifies a bootloader. The bootloader then verifies the application. Both transitions include a check.
hw-u1-concept-18.takeaway: A chain of trust connects startup stages through verification.

hw-u1-concept-19.title: Using a secret without revealing it
hw-u1-concept-19.body: A trusted execution environment, or TEE, can isolate sensitive operations and secrets from normal applications. An application can request an allowed operation without receiving the secret itself.
hw-u1-concept-19.example: An application sends a message to an isolated signing service. The service returns a signature while keeping the signing key inside its protected environment.
hw-u1-concept-19.takeaway: A trusted execution environment, or TEE, can isolate sensitive operations and secrets from normal applications.

hw-u1-concept-20.title: Reporting a weakness clearly
hw-u1-concept-20.body: Coordinated vulnerability disclosure starts by giving the responsible organisation enough information to investigate a weakness. A useful report identifies the affected product, the observed behaviour and how to reproduce it.
hw-u1-concept-20.example: A researcher reports the device model, firmware version and steps that demonstrate an unintended information leak.
hw-u1-concept-20.takeaway: Coordinated vulnerability disclosure starts by giving the responsible organisation enough information to investigate a weakness.

hw-u2-concept-16.title: What a capacitor does
hw-u2-concept-16.body: A capacitor stores electrical energy associated with separated charge. It can receive charge from a supply and later release energy into a connected circuit.
hw-u2-concept-16.example: A capacitor charges while connected to a supply. After the supply is removed, it briefly powers an indicator before the indicator fades.
hw-u2-concept-16.takeaway: A capacitor stores electrical energy associated with separated charge.

hw-u2-concept-17.title: Charging through a resistor
hw-u2-concept-17.body: Changing a capacitor’s voltage requires charge to move. When it charges through a resistor, the resistor limits current and the capacitor’s voltage rises gradually.
hw-u2-concept-17.example: An uncharged capacitor connects to a 3 V supply through a resistor. Its voltage starts near zero and rises towards 3 V.
hw-u2-concept-17.takeaway: Changing a capacitor’s voltage requires charge to move.

hw-u2-concept-18.title: Helping a chip through a brief current demand
hw-u2-concept-18.body: A chip’s current demand can rise quickly. A nearby decoupling capacitor, connected between supply and ground, helps provide brief current demands and reduces local supply disturbances.
hw-u2-concept-18.example: A processor suddenly becomes active. Its nearby capacitor supplies some current while the rest of the supply network responds.
hw-u2-concept-18.takeaway: A chip’s current demand can rise quickly.

hw-u2-concept-19.title: Understanding the limit of that support
hw-u2-concept-19.body: A capacitor stores a finite amount of energy. If it supplies a running circuit without being recharged, its stored energy decreases and its voltage falls.
hw-u2-concept-19.example: A capacitor helps a sensor through a short interruption. A longer interruption exhausts that support and the sensor stops working.
hw-u2-concept-19.takeaway: A capacitor stores a finite amount of energy.

hw-u2-concept-20.title: What an inductor does
hw-u2-concept-20.body: An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field associated with current. It opposes rapid changes in the current flowing through it.
hw-u2-concept-20.example: When a circuit tries to interrupt current through a coil suddenly, the coil can produce a voltage spike as its stored energy is released.
hw-u2-concept-20.takeaway: An inductor stores energy in a magnetic field associated with current.

hw-u2-concept-21.title: A diode’s direction matters
hw-u2-concept-21.body: A diode conducts much more readily in one direction than the other. Its orientation therefore affects current flow.
hw-u2-concept-21.example: In a simple battery–resistor–LED circuit, the LED normally lights in its forward direction. Reversing it prevents normal illumination.
hw-u2-concept-21.takeaway: A diode conducts much more readily in one direction than the other.

hw-u2-concept-22.title: Controlling a separate current path
hw-u2-concept-22.body: A transistor can work as an electrically controlled switch. In a suitable circuit, a small control signal switches a separate path supplying current to a load.
hw-u2-concept-22.example: A processor pin controls a transistor. The transistor switches an indicator’s supply current, so that current does not have to pass through the processor’s control pin.
hw-u2-concept-22.takeaway: A transistor can work as an electrically controlled switch.

hw-u2-concept-23.title: Producing the required supply voltage
hw-u2-concept-23.body: A voltage regulator maintains a specified output voltage within its operating limits. A regulator and decoupling capacitors have complementary jobs: regulation establishes the supply level, while decoupling helps with rapid local disturbances.
hw-u2-concept-23.example: A board accepts 9 V. A suitable regulator provides a 3.3 V rail, and nearby capacitors support the processor connected to that rail.
hw-u2-concept-23.takeaway: A voltage regulator maintains a specified output voltage within its operating limits.

hw-u2-concept-24.title: Recognising variation on a DC supply
hw-u2-concept-24.body: A DC supply maintains one polarity, but its voltage can still vary. Noise, ripple and temporary dips can occur on top of the normal DC level.
hw-u2-concept-24.example: A nominal 5 V rail briefly falls to 4.8 V and recovers. Its polarity stays the same, so it remains a DC supply with a disturbance.
hw-u2-concept-24.takeaway: A DC supply maintains one polarity, but its voltage can still vary.

hw-u2-concept-25.title: Letting devices take turns
hw-u2-concept-25.body: A push-pull output actively drives HIGH or LOW. A tristate output can also enter a high-impedance state, allowing another device to drive a shared wire.
hw-u2-concept-25.example: Device A sends data while device B disables its output. They reverse these roles when B needs to reply.
hw-u2-concept-25.takeaway: A push-pull output actively drives HIGH or LOW.

hw-u2-concept-26.title: Preserving fast signal details
hw-u2-concept-26.body: The oscilloscope and probe must both have enough bandwidth for the features being measured. A low-bandwidth probe can smooth fast transitions before the oscilloscope samples them.
hw-u2-concept-26.example: A fast oscilloscope receives a rounded waveform through an unsuitable probe. Increasing the sampling rate does not recover the detail lost through that probe.
hw-u2-concept-26.takeaway: The oscilloscope and probe must both have enough bandwidth for the features being measured.

hw-u2-concept-27.title: Capturing a supply disturbance
hw-u2-concept-27.body: An oscilloscope trigger selects an event around which to capture a waveform. A falling-edge trigger can target a supply dropping below a chosen voltage.
hw-u2-concept-27.example: A board normally runs at 3.3 V. Triggering on a downward crossing of 3.0 V helps capture occasional larger supply dips.
hw-u2-concept-27.takeaway: An oscilloscope trigger selects an event around which to capture a waveform.

hw-u3-concept-19.title: Matching the complete UART format
hw-u3-concept-19.body: UART settings specify speed and frame format. 8N1 means eight data bits, no parity bit and one stop bit.
hw-u3-concept-19.example: A device specified as 9600 8N1 needs 9,600 baud, eight data bits, no parity and one stop bit.
hw-u3-concept-19.takeaway: UART settings specify speed and frame format.

hw-u3-concept-20.title: Checking electrical compatibility separately
hw-u3-concept-20.body: Similar serial framing can use different electrical signals. RS-232 and low-voltage logic-level UART are not directly interchangeable merely because their communication settings match.
hw-u3-concept-20.example: Two interfaces both use 9600 8N1, but an RS-232 adapter’s signal voltages are unsuitable for a processor’s 3.3 V input.
hw-u3-concept-20.takeaway: Similar serial framing can use different electrical signals.

hw-u3-concept-21.title: Following SPI responses
hw-u3-concept-21.body: COPI carries data from the controller to the peripheral. CIPO carries data from the peripheral to the controller.
hw-u3-concept-21.example: A controller sends a sensor command on COPI. The sensor returns its measurement on CIPO.
hw-u3-concept-21.takeaway: COPI carries data from the controller to the peripheral.

hw-u3-concept-22.title: Selecting an I²C register before reading
hw-u3-concept-22.body: A register is a small numbered storage location inside a device. In a common I²C register-read sequence, the controller first writes the register number, then begins a read transfer to receive its contents.
hw-u3-concept-22.example: To read register 0x05, a controller selects the device, sends 0x05 as the register selection, then requests the data.
hw-u3-concept-22.takeaway: A register is a small numbered storage location inside a device.

hw-u3-concept-23.title: Observing pins without taking control
hw-u3-concept-23.body: JTAG boundary scan provides different operations. SAMPLE observes pin states during normal operation. EXTEST can take control of external connections and may interrupt normal operation.
hw-u3-concept-23.example: An engineer selects SAMPLE to inspect a running board’s signals without intentionally taking over its output pins.
hw-u3-concept-23.takeaway: JTAG boundary scan provides different operations.

hw-u3-concept-24.title: Recovering timing from the signal
hw-u3-concept-24.body: Some protocols encode timing information within their communication signals. Their receivers recover timing without a separate clock wire.
hw-u3-concept-24.example: A USB receiver uses information in the encoded signal to recover the timing needed to interpret its data.
hw-u3-concept-24.takeaway: Some protocols encode timing information within their communication signals.

hw-u4-concept-13.title: Choosing a useful documentation source
hw-u4-concept-13.body: Regulatory filings for some products contain internal photographs and technical documents. An FCC identifier can help locate the corresponding filing.
hw-u4-concept-13.example: A researcher searches a product’s FCC identifier and finds internal photographs that reveal its board layout.
hw-u4-concept-13.takeaway: Regulatory filings for some products contain internal photographs and technical documents.

hw-u4-concept-14.title: Understanding physical access to chip connections
hw-u4-concept-14.body: Chip packages expose connections differently. Some have projecting metal leads; others place pads or solder balls underneath the body. This affects how easily a probe or clip can reach them.
hw-u4-concept-14.example: An SOIC’s visible side leads may accept a suitable clip. A BGA’s hidden solder balls cannot be reached in the same way.

hw-u4-concept-15.title: Recognising a configurable connection
hw-u4-concept-15.body: A zero-ohm resistor acts approximately as an electrical link. Manufacturers can fit or omit it to select different configurations on the same board design.
hw-u4-concept-15.example: One product variant includes a zero-ohm link connecting a configuration pin to ground. Another variant omits that connection.
hw-u4-concept-15.takeaway: A zero-ohm resistor acts approximately as an electrical link.

hw-u4-concept-16.title: Following a trace between layers
hw-u4-concept-16.body: A trace carries a connection along a PCB layer. A via connects conductive features between layers, so a visible trace can continue through a route hidden inside the board.
hw-u4-concept-16.example: A trace leaves a processor, reaches a via and continues on an internal layer towards another component.
hw-u4-concept-16.takeaway: A trace carries a connection along a PCB layer.

hw-u4-concept-17.title: Checking for available firmware first
hw-u4-concept-17.body: A vendor’s update download may provide firmware suitable for initial analysis. Checking available software sources can avoid unnecessary physical extraction.
hw-u4-concept-17.example: A researcher finds an update for the correct model and hardware revision, then examines its contents before considering removal of the flash chip.
hw-u4-concept-17.takeaway: A vendor’s update download may provide firmware suitable for initial analysis.

hw-u4-concept-18.title: Interpreting a detected file format
hw-u4-concept-18.body: Firmware-analysis tools can recognise candidate formats from characteristic byte patterns, often called magic bytes. A detection suggests where to investigate; it does not prove that the entire file has that format.
hw-u4-concept-18.example: A tool detects a possible filesystem halfway through an update. The researcher examines that region and checks its boundaries and contents.
hw-u4-concept-18.takeaway: Firmware-analysis tools can recognise candidate formats from characteristic byte patterns, often called magic bytes.

hw-u1-q01.title: What is an embedded system?
hw-u1-q01.statement: Which component is an embedded system?

options.a: The plastic casing of a thermostat
options.b: The controller that reads temperature and switches the heating
options.c: The printed installation instructions

hw-u1-q01.hint: Look for the component that processes information and controls something.
hw-u1-q01.explanation: The controller performs computing tasks within the thermostat.
solutionSteps: The controller performs computing tasks within the thermostat.
Choose B: The controller that reads temperature and switches the heating.

hw-u1-q02.title: Following information through a device
hw-u1-q02.statement: In a thermostat, which component decides whether the measured temperature requires heating?

options.a: The temperature sensor
options.b: The heating relay
options.c: The processor

hw-u1-q02.hint: Measuring, deciding, and acting are different jobs.
hw-u1-q02.explanation: The processor uses the sensor’s measurement to decide what the output should do.
solutionSteps: The processor uses the sensor’s measurement to decide what the output should do.
Choose C: The processor.

hw-u1-q03.title: Remembering after power is removed
hw-u1-q03.statement: A device must remember its calibration after its battery is removed. Which memory is suitable?

options.a: Flash memory
options.b: Ordinary RAM
options.c: Either type retains data equally well without power

hw-u1-q03.hint: Consider whether the stored information must survive a complete power loss.
hw-u1-q03.explanation: Flash is nonvolatile. Ordinary RAM loses its contents when power is removed.
solutionSteps: Flash is nonvolatile. Ordinary RAM loses its contents when power is removed.
Choose A: Flash memory.

hw-u1-q04.title: Recognizing firmware
hw-u1-q04.statement: Which item is firmware in a smart lock?

options.a: A record of yesterday’s door openings
options.b: The instructions that check a credential and operate the lock
options.c: The serial number printed on its case

hw-u1-q04.hint: Look for executable instructions that determine the device’s behavior.
hw-u1-q04.explanation: Firmware contains the instructions that run the device.
solutionSteps: Firmware contains the instructions that run the device.
Choose B: The instructions that check a credential and operate the lock.

hw-u1-q05.title: Understanding startup
hw-u1-q05.statement: In this startup arrangement, which component prepares and loads the application firmware?

options.a: The application’s settings file
options.b: The temperature sensor
options.c: The bootloader

hw-u1-q05.hint: Identify the stage between the earliest boot code and the application.
hw-u1-q05.explanation: The bootloader prepares the transition to the main firmware.
solutionSteps: The bootloader prepares the transition to the main firmware.
Choose C: The bootloader.

hw-u1-q06.title: Identifying an asset
hw-u1-q06.statement: An attacker wants to obtain a smart lock’s secret access credential. What is the asset in this scenario?

options.a: The secret credential
options.b: The tool used to open the case
options.c: The attacker’s workbench

hw-u1-q06.hint: Ask what valuable thing the attacker is trying to obtain.
hw-u1-q06.explanation: The credential is the information that needs protection.
solutionSteps: The credential is the information that needs protection.
Choose A: The secret credential.

hw-u1-q07.title: Protecting confidentiality
hw-u1-q07.statement: Someone copies a device’s secret key but leaves the device working normally. Which property has clearly been violated?

options.a: Availability
options.b: Confidentiality
options.c: Physical durability

hw-u1-q07.hint: Focus on who can now see the secret.
hw-u1-q07.explanation: The key has been disclosed to an unauthorized person. Normal operation does not undo that disclosure.
solutionSteps: The key has been disclosed to an unauthorized person. Normal operation does not undo that disclosure.
Choose B: Confidentiality.

hw-u1-q08.title: Protecting integrity
hw-u1-q08.statement: An attacker changes a sensor’s alarm threshold without permission. Which property is directly affected?

options.a: Confidentiality
options.b: Availability
options.c: Integrity

hw-u1-q08.hint: Was information exposed, changed, or made unavailable?
hw-u1-q08.explanation: The attacker modified a setting that influences the device’s behavior.
solutionSteps: The attacker modified a setting that influences the device’s behavior.
Choose C: Integrity.

hw-u1-q09.title: Authenticating firmware
hw-u1-q09.statement: Which check directly supports accepting only firmware authorized by the vendor?

options.a: Verify its digital signature using a trusted vendor key
options.b: Check that the filename contains the vendor’s name
options.c: Check that its file size matches the previous version

hw-u1-q09.hint: Names and sizes can be copied without the vendor’s authorization.
hw-u1-q09.explanation: A valid signature under the trusted key provides evidence of authorization and protects against undetected modification.
solutionSteps: A valid signature under the trusted key provides evidence of authorization and protects against undetected modification.
Choose A: Verify its digital signature using a trusted vendor key.

hw-u1-q10.title: Considering the attacker’s access
hw-u1-q10.statement: A device moves from a locked cabinet to an unattended public area. Which assumption most needs reviewing?

options.a: Whether its firmware uses variables
options.b: Whether an attacker can physically access the hardware
options.c: Whether its processor executes instructions

hw-u1-q10.hint: Consider what the new location allows someone to do.
hw-u1-q10.explanation: Physical access becomes more plausible and may expose additional attack paths.
solutionSteps: Physical access becomes more plausible and may expose additional attack paths.
Choose B: Whether an attacker can physically access the hardware.

hw-u1-q11.title: Recognizing multiple access paths
hw-u1-q11.statement: A device’s network connection is disabled, but its internal debug interface remains accessible. What can we conclude?

options.a: Every attack path has been removed
options.b: The debug interface becomes encrypted automatically
options.c: A physical interaction path still remains

hw-u1-q11.hint: Removing one entrance does not establish what happened to the others.
hw-u1-q11.explanation: The network path is removed, but the debug interface must be assessed separately.
solutionSteps: The network path is removed, but the debug interface must be assessed separately.
Choose C: A physical interaction path still remains.

hw-u1-q12.title: Stating a useful threat
hw-u1-q12.statement: Which description gives the clearest threat scenario?

options.a: A person with the device could use an exposed interface to copy private records
options.b: The device might be insecure
options.c: The device contains several chips

hw-u1-q12.hint: Look for who can act, what they can reach, and what could go wrong.
hw-u1-q12.explanation: It identifies physical access, private records, and unauthorized copying.
solutionSteps: It identifies physical access, private records, and unauthorized copying.
Choose A: A person with the device could use an exposed interface to copy private records.

hw-u1-q13.title: Understanding alternative attack paths
hw-u1-q13.statement: A secret can be obtained through interface A or interface B. Interface A is blocked. What follows?

options.a: Both paths are now blocked
options.b: Interface B must still be assessed
options.c: The secret is automatically replaced

hw-u1-q13.hint: “OR” means the attacker needs only one successful route.
hw-u1-q13.explanation: Blocking one alternative does not remove the other.
solutionSteps: Blocking one alternative does not remove the other.
Choose B: Interface B must still be assessed.

hw-u1-q14.title: Understanding required combinations
hw-u1-q14.statement: A modeled attack requires opening the enclosure and authenticating to the service interface. The attacker opens the enclosure but cannot authenticate. What can we conclude?

options.a: Opening the enclosure completes the attack
options.b: The entire device is secure against every attack
options.c: This modeled path is incomplete

hw-u1-q14.hint: Distinguish stopping one path from proving that no other path exists.
hw-u1-q14.explanation: One required condition is missing. That blocks this path, without proving overall security.
solutionSteps: One required condition is missing. That blocks this path, without proving overall security.
Choose C: This modeled path is incomplete.

hw-u1-q15.title: Combining protection, detection, and response
hw-u1-q15.statement: A device already has a locked enclosure and an opening sensor, but nothing happens when the sensor triggers. Which addition supplies a response?

options.a: Suspend sensitive operations and notify the operator when the alarm triggers
options.b: Add another sensor that is also ignored
options.c: Make the enclosure label larger

hw-u1-q15.hint: A response changes what the system does after detection.
hw-u1-q15.explanation: It connects detection to a defined action, adding the missing response.
solutionSteps: It connects detection to a defined action, adding the missing response.
Choose A: Suspend sensitive operations and notify the operator when the alarm triggers.

hw-u2-q01.title: Understanding voltage
hw-u2-q01.statement: A meter reads 5 V between a supply pin and ground. What does this describe?

options.a: The amount of data stored in the device
options.b: The electrical potential difference between those points
options.c: The current through every component

hw-u2-q01.explanation: The reading describes a potential difference, not current or stored information.
solutionSteps: The reading describes a potential difference, not current or stored information.
Choose B: The electrical potential difference between those points.

hw-u2-q02.title: Understanding current
hw-u2-q02.statement: A device draws 0.2 A from a suitable supply rated for up to 1 A. How much current is it drawing?

options.b: 1 A

hw-u2-q02.hint: Separate the supply’s capacity from the device’s actual demand.
hw-u2-q02.explanation: The rating gives the supply’s capacity; the stated load draws 0.2 A.
solutionSteps: The rating gives the supply’s capacity; the stated load draws 0.2 A.
Choose A: 0.2 A.

hw-u2-q03.title: Understanding resistance
hw-u2-q03.statement: A resistor is changed from 1 kΩ to 4 kΩ while the voltage across it stays constant. What happens to its current?

options.a: It increases
options.b: It stays the same
options.c: It decreases

hw-u2-q03.hint: More resistance means less current when voltage is unchanged.
hw-u2-q03.explanation: Increasing resistance reduces current at a fixed voltage.
solutionSteps: Increasing resistance reduces current at a fixed voltage.
Choose C: It decreases.

hw-u2-q04.title: Applying Ohm’s law
hw-u2-q04.statement: What current flows through an ideal 2,000 Ω resistor with 4 V across it?

options.a: 0.5 mA
options.b: 2 mA
options.c: 8 mA

hw-u2-q04.hint: Divide the voltage by the resistance, then convert amperes to milliamperes.
solutionSteps: 4 / 2000 = 0.002 A, which is 2 mA.
Choose B: 2 mA.

hw-u2-q05.title: Relating voltage and current to power
hw-u2-q05.statement: A device draws 0.2 A at 5 V. What electrical power does it receive?

options.a: 1 W

solutionSteps: Choose A: 1 W.

hw-u2-q06.title: Sharing a reference
hw-u2-q06.statement: Two devices exchange a single-ended signal without an established common reference. What problem can occur?

options.a: Their firmware becomes identical
options.b: Their supply ratings automatically match
options.c: The receiver misinterprets the signal voltage

hw-u2-q06.hint: A voltage reading depends on the reference used.
hw-u2-q06.explanation: Different reference potentials can change the voltage seen by the receiver.
solutionSteps: Different reference potentials can change the voltage seen by the receiver.
Choose C: The receiver misinterprets the signal voltage.

hw-u2-q07.title: Interpreting logic levels
hw-u2-q07.statement: LOW is guaranteed at or below 0.8 V and HIGH at or above 2.0 V. How should a 1.4 V input be classified?

options.a: Guaranteed HIGH
options.b: Neither guaranteed LOW nor guaranteed HIGH
options.c: Guaranteed LOW

hw-u2-q07.hint: Compare the voltage with both guaranteed ranges.
hw-u2-q07.explanation: It lies between the specified LOW and HIGH ranges.
solutionSteps: It lies between the specified LOW and HIGH ranges.
Choose B: Neither guaranteed LOW nor guaranteed HIGH.

hw-u2-q08.title: Checking electrical compatibility
hw-u2-q08.statement: A transmitter produces 5 V signals. The receiver’s input has an absolute maximum of 3.6 V and is not 5 V tolerant. Which approach is appropriate?

options.a: Use suitable level translation within the receiver’s specifications
options.b: Connect directly because both devices use digital signals
options.c: Connect directly because 5 V clearly represents HIGH

hw-u2-q08.hint: Check electrical limits before interpreting the logical value.
hw-u2-q08.explanation: Level translation can provide compatible signal voltages. A direct 5 V connection exceeds the stated limit.
solutionSteps: Level translation can provide compatible signal voltages. A direct 5 V connection exceeds the stated limit.
Choose A: Use suitable level translation within the receiver’s specifications.

hw-u2-q09.title: Recognizing a floating input
hw-u2-q09.statement: A disconnected input changes state unpredictably. Which explanation best fits?

options.a: It must be receiving valid messages
options.b: High impedance guarantees a LOW reading
options.c: The input is floating

hw-u2-q09.hint: Ask what is establishing the pin’s voltage.
hw-u2-q09.explanation: Without a driver or bias, the input may have no defined logic level.
solutionSteps: Without a driver or bias, the input may have no defined logic level.
Choose C: The input is floating.

hw-u2-q10.title: Giving a released line a defined state
hw-u2-q10.statement: Two open-drain devices share a pulled-up line. One releases it and the other pulls LOW. What is the line’s expected state?

options.a: HIGH
options.b: LOW
options.c: Halfway between HIGH and LOW

hw-u2-q10.hint: Releasing the line is different from actively driving it HIGH.
hw-u2-q10.explanation: The active pull-down holds the line LOW despite the pull-up.
solutionSteps: The active pull-down holds the line LOW despite the pull-up.
Choose B: LOW.

hw-u2-q11.title: Measuring a supply voltage
hw-u2-q11.statement: Which setup measures a board’s supply voltage?

options.a: Voltage mode, with probes between the supply rail and ground
options.b: Continuity mode, with probes across the powered supply
options.c: Current mode, with probes directly across the supply and ground

hw-u2-q11.hint: Match the meter mode to the quantity being measured.
hw-u2-q11.explanation: Voltage mode measures the difference between the rail and ground. Current mode across a supply can create a short circuit.
solutionSteps: Voltage mode measures the difference between the rail and ground. Current mode across a supply can create a short circuit.
Choose A: Voltage mode, with probes between the supply rail and ground.

hw-u2-q12.title: Interpreting continuity
hw-u2-q12.statement: Two test points on an unpowered board produce a continuity beep. What is the strongest supported conclusion?

options.a: They must be joined by one uninterrupted copper trace
options.b: They must carry the same digital protocol
options.c: A sufficiently low-resistance path exists between them

hw-u2-q12.hint: Separate what the instrument measured from how the board might be constructed.
hw-u2-q12.explanation: The beep indicates low resistance according to the meter’s threshold, without identifying the route.
solutionSteps: The beep indicates low resistance according to the meter’s threshold, without identifying the route.
Choose C: A sufficiently low-resistance path exists between them.

hw-u2-q13.title: Finding a brief voltage disturbance
hw-u2-q13.statement: A board resets unexpectedly, but its supply looks steady on a multimeter. Which measurement is most useful next?

options.a: Measure only the enclosure’s resistance
options.b: Observe the supply waveform with an oscilloscope around the reset
options.c: Repeat the same steady reading and assume the supply cannot be involved

hw-u2-q13.hint: The suspected problem may exist only briefly.
hw-u2-q13.explanation: A time-resolved measurement can reveal short disturbances hidden by the multimeter’s display.
solutionSteps: A time-resolved measurement can reveal short disturbances hidden by the multimeter’s display.
Choose B: Observe the supply waveform with an oscilloscope around the reset.

hw-u2-q14.title: Choosing a logic analyzer
hw-u2-q14.statement: You want to compare the order of transitions on eight digital lines. Which tool is most directly suited?

options.a: A suitably configured logic analyzer
options.b: A multimeter in continuity mode
options.c: A power supply’s current-limit control

hw-u2-q14.hint: The task concerns several digital sequences rather than detailed voltage shape.
hw-u2-q14.explanation: A logic analyzer can capture and compare multiple digital channels.
solutionSteps: A logic analyzer can capture and compare multiple digital channels.
Choose A: A suitably configured logic analyzer.

hw-u2-q15.title: Recognizing a missed event
hw-u2-q15.statement: A logic analyzer samples every 1 microsecond. A pulse may last only 0.1 microseconds. Its capture shows no pulse. What can you conclude?

options.a: The pulse definitely never happened
options.b: Every pulse must last at least 1 microsecond
options.c: The capture may have missed the pulse

hw-u2-q15.hint: Compare the event’s duration with the gaps between observations.
hw-u2-q15.explanation: The pulse could fit between samples. A suitable faster capture and appropriate instrument specifications are needed to investigate it reliably.
solutionSteps: The pulse could fit between samples. A suitable faster capture and appropriate instrument specifications are needed to investigate it reliably.
Choose C: The capture may have missed the pulse.

hw-u3-q01.title: A connector is not a protocol
hw-u3-q01.statement: You find an unfamiliar four-pin connector. What should you establish before connecting an adapter?

options.a: Whether the adapter physically fits
options.b: The pin assignments and electrical requirements
options.c: Whether both boards have the same colour

hw-u3-q01.hint: Physical compatibility does not establish electrical compatibility.
hw-u3-q01.explanation: Identify what each pin does and its voltage requirements before connecting anything.
solutionSteps: Identify what each pin does and its voltage requirements before connecting anything.
Choose B: The pin assignments and electrical requirements.

hw-u3-q02.title: UART transmit and receive
hw-u3-q02.statement: Which connection lets an adapter receive messages transmitted by a board?

options.a: Board TX → adapter RX
options.b: Board TX → adapter TX
options.c: Board RX → adapter RX

hw-u3-q02.hint: Follow the message from the transmitter to the receiver.
hw-u3-q02.explanation: The board transmits through TX, and the adapter receives through RX.
solutionSteps: The board transmits through TX, and the adapter receives through RX.
Choose A: Board TX → adapter RX.

hw-u3-q03.title: Matching UART timing
hw-u3-q03.statement: Documentation specifies 38,400 baud, but your adapter uses 9,600. What is the first setting to correct?

options.a: The connector’s pin count
options.b: The board’s supply-current limit
options.c: The adapter’s baud rate

hw-u3-q03.explanation: Set the adapter to the documented baud rate, then check the remaining UART settings if necessary.
solutionSteps: Set the adapter to the documented baud rate, then check the remaining UART settings if necessary.
Choose C: The adapter’s baud rate.

hw-u3-q04.title: Unreadable output is not a diagnosis
hw-u3-q04.statement: A terminal shows unreadable characters. Which conclusion is justified?

options.a: The device definitely encrypts its output
options.b: The settings and data format need checking
options.c: The device has no functioning processor

hw-u3-q04.hint: Several different causes can produce the same observation.
hw-u3-q04.explanation: Check the communication settings and expected format before deciding what the output means.
solutionSteps: Check the communication settings and expected format before deciding what the output means.
Choose B: The settings and data format need checking.

hw-u3-q05.title: SPI uses a shared clock
hw-u3-q05.statement: Why must a decoder observe the SPI clock as well as the data?

options.a: The clock provides timing for interpreting the bits
options.b: The clock identifies the manufacturer
options.c: The clock stores the transferred information

hw-u3-q05.explanation: Data values must be interpreted at the appropriate moments relative to the clock.
solutionSteps: Data values must be interpreted at the appropriate moments relative to the clock.
Choose A: The clock provides timing for interpreting the bits.

hw-u3-q06.title: Selecting an SPI target
hw-u3-q06.statement: A flash chip and a display have separate active-low selects. The flash select is LOW and the display select is HIGH. Which is selected?

options.a: Both devices
options.b: The display
options.c: The flash chip

hw-u3-q06.hint: For an active-low signal, LOW means active.
hw-u3-q06.explanation: The flash is selected. This assumes the documented active-low behaviour.
solutionSteps: The flash is selected. This assumes the documented active-low behaviour.
Choose C: The flash chip.

hw-u3-q07.title: Selecting the correct SPI mode
hw-u3-q07.statement: You have identified the SPI wires, but decoded values disagree with known transfers. What should you check next?

options.a: Whether the connector has enough unused pins
options.b: Whether the decoder’s clock settings match the device
options.c: Whether the chip-select wire can replace the clock

hw-u3-q07.hint: Correct wires do not guarantee correct sampling.
hw-u3-q07.explanation: Check the clock mode, along with other documented settings such as bit order.
solutionSteps: Check the clock mode, along with other documented settings such as bit order.
Choose B: Whether the decoder’s clock settings match the device.

hw-u3-q08.title: I²C’s two shared signals
hw-u3-q08.statement: Every device releases SDA, but the required pull-up is missing. What can happen?

options.a: SDA may lack a reliable HIGH level
options.b: SDA automatically becomes a UART transmitter
options.c: Every device receives a new address

hw-u3-q08.hint: Releasing a line does not itself drive it HIGH.
hw-u3-q08.explanation: Without the required pull-up, the released line may float rather than reach a dependable HIGH level.
solutionSteps: Without the required pull-up, the released line may float rather than reach a dependable HIGH level.
Choose A: SDA may lack a reliable HIGH level.

hw-u3-q09.title: I²C addresses
hw-u3-q09.statement: Two sensors share an address and must be controlled independently. Which solution can resolve the conflict?

options.a: Increase the supply voltage
options.b: Rename the sensors in your notes
options.c: Configure one sensor to use a different supported address

hw-u3-q09.hint: The bus uses the transmitted address, not your label.
hw-u3-q09.explanation: A supported address change gives each target a distinct address.
solutionSteps: A supported address change gives each target a distinct address.
Choose C: Configure one sensor to use a different supported address.

hw-u3-q10.title: What an acknowledgement tells you
hw-u3-q10.statement: An address receives an ACK. What can you conclude from that observation alone?

options.a: The target completed every requested operation
options.b: Something on the bus acknowledged that address
options.c: The target’s firmware is authentic

hw-u3-q10.hint: Keep the conclusion limited to the event you observed.
hw-u3-q10.explanation: The ACK establishes an acknowledgement at that point in the transfer, not broader correctness or authenticity.
solutionSteps: The ACK establishes an acknowledgement at that point in the transfer, not broader correctness or authenticity.
Choose B: Something on the bus acknowledged that address.

hw-u3-q11.title: Distinguishing bus arrangements
hw-u3-q11.statement: Two chips share a clock and separate outgoing/incoming data lines. Each has its own select wire. Which interpretation best fits?

options.a: Typical four-wire SPI
options.b: Basic UART
options.c: Typical two-wire I²C

hw-u3-q11.hint: Look at how the controller selects a target.
hw-u3-q11.explanation: Shared clock/data signals with separate chip selects fit the common SPI arrangement. Confirm against documentation or captured traffic.
solutionSteps: Shared clock/data signals with separate chip selects fit the common SPI arrangement. Confirm against documentation or captured traffic.
Choose A: Typical four-wire SPI.

hw-u3-q12.title: CAN uses a differential pair
hw-u3-q12.statement: You identify CANH and CANL on a device. Which connection approach matches those signals?

options.a: Treat CANH as UART TX and CANL as UART RX
options.b: Connect either line directly to an arbitrary logic input
options.c: Use a compatible CAN interface with a suitable transceiver

hw-u3-q12.hint: Both wires form one differential signalling pair.
hw-u3-q12.explanation: A suitable CAN interface handles the bus’s electrical signalling and protocol.
solutionSteps: A suitable CAN interface handles the bus’s electrical signalling and protocol.
Choose C: Use a compatible CAN interface with a suitable transceiver.

hw-u3-q13.title: USB identification is a reported description
hw-u3-q13.statement: A device reports a familiar product identifier. What does that establish by itself?

options.a: The hardware is certainly genuine
options.b: The device reported that identifier
options.c: Its firmware cannot have changed

hw-u3-q13.hint: A description supplied by a device is a claim from that device.
hw-u3-q13.explanation: Enumeration reveals reported identity and capabilities; stronger authenticity claims require additional evidence.
solutionSteps: Enumeration reveals reported identity and capabilities; stronger authenticity claims require additional evidence.
Choose B: The device reported that identifier.

hw-u3-q14.title: An SD-related interface is not always storage
hw-u3-q14.statement: A datasheet describes a component as an “SDIO wireless module.” What is the best interpretation?

options.a: It uses SDIO to communicate with a wireless component
options.b: It must contain the device’s main firmware storage
options.c: It must be a removable memory card

hw-u3-q14.hint: Use the component’s documented function as well as its interface.
hw-u3-q14.explanation: SDIO supports input/output functions; the interface name alone does not establish storage.
solutionSteps: SDIO supports input/output functions; the interface name alone does not establish storage.
Choose A: It uses SDIO to communicate with a wireless component.

hw-u3-q15.title: Capturing a parallel bus
hw-u3-q15.statement: You capture the clock and one data line of an eight-bit parallel bus. Can you reconstruct arbitrary complete bytes from that capture alone?

options.a: Yes, because the clock contains the missing bits
options.b: Yes, because every data line carries the same value
options.c: No, because seven data bits were not observed

hw-u3-q15.hint: Parallel transfer distributes information across several wires.
hw-u3-q15.explanation: The capture lacks the other data lines needed to reconstruct each complete byte.
solutionSteps: The capture lacks the other data lines needed to reconstruct each complete byte.
Choose C: No, because seven data bits were not observed.

hw-u3-q16.title: JTAG testing and debugging
hw-u3-q16.statement: A JTAG boundary-scan operation succeeds. Which conclusion is justified?

options.a: All firmware can definitely be read
options.b: That boundary-scan operation is available
options.c: Every security restriction is disabled

hw-u3-q16.hint: One working function does not prove that all functions are available.
hw-u3-q16.explanation: Boundary-scan access and processor-debug access are distinct capabilities.
solutionSteps: Boundary-scan access and processor-debug access are distinct capabilities.
Choose B: That boundary-scan operation is available.

hw-u3-q17.title: Choosing capture equipment
hw-u3-q17.statement: Your analyser shows no useful traffic on a fast interface. What should you check before concluding that the interface is inactive?

options.a: Whether the equipment and configuration can capture that interface
options.b: Whether the board has a printed product name
options.c: Whether another connector has fewer pins

hw-u3-q17.hint: Missing evidence can result from an unsuitable measurement.
hw-u3-q17.explanation: Check signal compatibility, probing, sampling capability and configuration before interpreting an empty capture.
solutionSteps: Check signal compatibility, probing, sampling capability and configuration before interpreting an empty capture.
Choose A: Whether the equipment and configuration can capture that interface.

hw-u3-q18.title: Combining interface evidence
hw-u3-q18.statement: You observe two pulled-up lines. One carries clock pulses; the other carries addresses and acknowledgements. What is the strongest next step?

options.a: Treat the lines as CANH/CANL because there are two
options.b: Connect an adapter without checking voltage compatibility
options.c: Test an I²C interpretation against documentation and captured transfers

hw-u3-q18.hint: Combine the electrical behaviour with the structure of the messages.
hw-u3-q18.explanation: The combined evidence supports I²C. Documentation and consistent decoding can strengthen that identification.
solutionSteps: The combined evidence supports I²C. Documentation and consistent decoding can strengthen that identification.
Choose C: Test an I²C interpretation against documentation and captured transfers.

hw-u4-q01.title: Identify the exact device
hw-u4-q01.statement: Which record best helps you find documentation for your particular board?

options.a: Product name alone
options.b: Product name, model identifier and board revision
options.c: Case colour alone

hw-u4-q01.hint: Record information that distinguishes one hardware version from another.
hw-u4-q01.explanation: Model and revision details reduce the risk of applying documentation to the wrong hardware.
solutionSteps: Model and revision details reduce the risk of applying documentation to the wrong hardware.
Choose B: Product name, model identifier and board revision.

hw-u4-q02.title: Record the original arrangement
hw-u4-q02.statement: You need to remove several similar internal cables. What should you do first?

options.a: Record where each cable connects and its orientation
options.b: Disconnect them and rely on memory
options.c: Assume interchangeable plugs mean interchangeable functions

hw-u4-q02.hint: Preserve information that may disappear when you disassemble the device.
hw-u4-q02.explanation: A record makes later reconstruction and comparison more reliable.
solutionSteps: A record makes later reconstruction and comparison more reliable.
Choose A: Record where each cable connects and its orientation.

hw-u4-q03.title: Use component markings as evidence
hw-u4-q03.statement: A search result matches part of a chip’s marking but shows a different package. What should you do?

options.a: Accept it because some letters match
options.b: Assume the package has no relevance
options.c: Treat it as uncertain and check other identifying details

hw-u4-q03.hint: A good identification should explain more than one observation.
hw-u4-q03.explanation: A partial marking match is a lead; inconsistent physical details need investigation.
solutionSteps: A partial marking match is a lead; inconsistent physical details need investigation.
Choose C: Treat it as uncertain and check other identifying details.

hw-u4-q04.title: Package shape does not establish function
hw-u4-q04.statement: You identify a large BGA package. What additional evidence best establishes its function?

options.a: Its size alone
options.b: A verified part identification and datasheet
options.c: Its distance from the board’s edge alone

hw-u4-q04.hint: Physical construction and electronic function are different properties.
hw-u4-q04.explanation: The package narrows physical possibilities; the identified part and documentation explain its function.
solutionSteps: The package narrows physical possibilities; the identified part and documentation explain its function.
Choose B: A verified part identification and datasheet.

hw-u4-q05.title: Read pinouts in the correct orientation
hw-u4-q05.statement: A datasheet provides a bottom-view pinout, but you are looking at the chip from above. What should you do before identifying a pin?

options.a: Account for the viewing direction and orientation marker
options.b: Copy the drawing directly without changing perspective
options.c: Ignore orientation because pin numbers are interchangeable

hw-u4-q05.hint: The same physical connection appears in a different position when viewed from the opposite side.
hw-u4-q05.explanation: Match the documented perspective to the physical component before assigning signals.
solutionSteps: Match the documented perspective to the physical component before assigning signals.
Choose A: Account for the viewing direction and orientation marker.

hw-u4-q06.title: Interpret continuity cautiously
hw-u4-q06.statement: Two points produce a continuity beep. What is the most careful conclusion?

options.a: They must be the same signal with no component between them
options.b: They must both be ground
options.c: A sufficiently low-resistance path exists under the test conditions

hw-u4-q06.hint: The instrument detects an electrical condition, not the complete route.
hw-u4-q06.explanation: Inspect the circuit and consult documentation before describing the exact connection.
solutionSteps: Inspect the circuit and consult documentation before describing the exact connection.
Choose C: A sufficiently low-resistance path exists under the test conditions.

hw-u4-q07.title: Build a map with confidence levels
hw-u4-q07.statement: You suspect a test pad connects to UART TX, but have not verified the route or signal. How should you record it?

options.a: “Confirmed UART TX”
options.b: “Possible UART TX; verification needed”
options.c: “Unused pad”
